name: 自家製麺 天狗 (Jikaseimen Tengu)

claims.text: This is a homemade-noodle (jikaseimen) shop centered on udon and soba (wheat and buckwheat noodles) plus in-house thin wheat 'sasamen' noodles. With fresh wheat noodles made and boiled on-site, flour dust and shared noodle-boiling water make heavy gluten cross-contamination effectively unavoidable. Not celiac-safe.

The broths are a Kyoto-style dashi typically seasoned with soy sauce, and there are curry-dashi dishes and tempura items as well. Most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so the broths and seasonings should be assumed to contain wheat.

Dishes documented in sources rely on dashi (typically bonito/fish-based), pork, egg (poached egg, oyako-don), and shrimp tempura, so the broths and most dishes are not vegan. Vegan suitability is unconfirmed and should be checked directly with the shop.

Reviewers describe friendly, attentive staff (including a charming guest comment notebook the staff write back into), which may make it easier to ask questions about ingredients in person, though no allergen accommodations are documented.

This is a one-person counter kitchen where the owner mills, rolls, cuts, and boils soba in the same small workspace. There is no documented gluten-free protocol, and cross-contact in a shop this size is likely. Celiac diners should not assume safety and would need to confirm directly.

Although the noodles are 100% buckwheat (十割そば) with no wheat binder, the soba is served with a tsuyu/mentsuyu dipping broth and light soy sauce (薄口醤油), both of which typically contain wheat. The owner explicitly suggests eating the soba dipped in mentsuyu or drizzled with light soy sauce.

The tsuyu is described as a Kanto-style kaeshi base served alongside light soy sauce — standard Japanese soy-based seasonings that usually include wheat, so the dish as served is not celiac-safe despite the wheat-free noodles.
The soba tsuyu is a traditional Japanese dashi-based broth, which typically contains bonito (fish), so the soba as served is not vegan. The sources surface no vegan-specific accommodations.
The noodles themselves are 100% buckwheat (十割そば) with no wheat flour added, so the wheat in this dish comes only from the dipping broth and soy sauce — not from the soba.
Everything is made to order by a single owner at the counter, so it is easy to speak with him directly about ingredients before ordering.

name: 熟成豚 かわむら (Jukuseibuta Kawamura)

claims.text: This is a tonkatsu specialist: pork is coated in wheat panko (from the Nakaya Panko Factory in Tokyo) and deep-fried, so it is not celiac-safe. There is no indication of a gluten-free menu or a dedicated fryer.
The breading is wheat panko and the cutlets are deep-fried, meaning gluten is present throughout the core cooking process.
Among the table condiments is a Yakushima ago-dashi soy sauce; most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat, so it should be treated as containing gluten.
Sauces offered include a soy-based ago-dashi shoyu and a demi-glace-style sauce, both wheat/soy-derived rather than gluten-free.

The menu is centered entirely on deep-fried pork cutlets, and accompaniments include miso soup and pork-based sides, so there are no vegan mains. The frying oil includes lard, making the deep-fryer unsuitable for vegan diners.

This is a Showa-retro kissaten built around coffee, light meals, and fried/breaded items. Wheat is pervasive (toast, royal toast, spaghetti, omurice, fried rice, curry roux, sandwiches), and there is no documented gluten-free menu, dedicated prep, or allergen handling. Anyone with celiac disease should treat it as unsuitable.
Yakimeshi (fried rice) and other savory plates are typically seasoned with Japanese soy sauce, which almost always contains wheat. No wheat-free seasoning or substitution is documented.

The menu centers on egg, dairy, and meat: cream soda, cream coffee, omurice, an egg-topped curry, mixed sandwiches, and toast. There is no documented vegan option and shared griddle/cookware makes cross-contact likely. Not suitable for strict vegans without confirming directly with the shop.
Regulars describe the owner and his mother as genuinely kind and attentive, so it is worth asking them directly about ingredients if you have dietary needs.
This is a tonkatsu specialist: the pork cutlets are coated in wheat-flour dredge and panko (wheat breadcrumbs) and deep-fried, so the dish is inherently wheat-based and not celiac-safe.
Even the egg specialty (玉かつ / tamago-katsu) is a breaded, deep-fried item, meaning the shared fryer carries breaded wheat coating; no gluten-free preparation or dedicated fryer is documented.
The house uses cholesterol-free rapeseed oil rather than lard, but this concerns the fat type, not gluten; the oil still fries wheat-breaded cutlets, so cross-contact with gluten remains.

The menu centers on tonkatsu with a house tonkatsu sauce and house ponzu, and ponzu/sauce in Japanese cooking typically involve soy sauce, which usually contains wheat; no wheat-free soy product is documented.

This is a pork tonkatsu specialist; no vegan or vegetarian main is documented. A bagna cauda of organic Kyoto vegetables is served, but bagna cauda is traditionally made with anchovy and is not vegan, and it is plated in a kitchen handling pork and fried wheat coating.

Frying is done in cholesterol-free rapeseed oil instead of lard, and sauces are made in-house without chemical seasonings, which can help diners who want to know exactly what is in the food, though this does not make any dish gluten-free or vegan.

This is an okonomiyaki and teppanyaki shop, and it is not celiac-safe. The okonomiyaki and yakisoba are built on wheat flour, the batter is bound with bonito-kombu dashi and chicken stock, and dishes are finished with a blend of Kyoto, Osaka, and Hiroshima okonomiyaki sauces that contain soy and wheat. There is heavy wheat, soy, and dashi presence throughout, and no gluten-free accommodation is documented.
Everything is cooked on a shared teppan griddle alongside wheat-based okonomiyaki and yakisoba, so cross-contact with gluten is essentially unavoidable even on non-batter items.
The finishing sauces blend Kyoto, Osaka, and Hiroshima okonomiyaki sauces, which are soy- and wheat-containing; most Japanese soy sauce is brewed with wheat.
Spicy items such as the beef-tendon suji-yaki use a doubanjiang and yanyanjiang (chili-bean paste) blend, which commonly contains soy and wheat.

The shop is known for a range of vegetable-forward small plates, but the kitchen relies heavily on bonito-kombu dashi, chicken stock, pork fat, and eggs, so vegetable dishes are not inherently vegan and should be confirmed dish by dish with the owner.
All cooking is done on a shared teppan also used for pork, beef, and shrimp, creating animal-product cross-contact for any plant-based order.
The owner Kawamura and his wife run the shop personally and are warm and talkative, so diners with dietary questions can speak directly with the people who source and cook the food.
Ingredients are carefully selected and bought in person from suppliers, so staff can speak knowledgeably about what goes into each dish.

name: かつかつとんとん (Katsukatsu Tonton)

claims.text: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. Tonkatsu is breaded in wheat flour and panko before deep-frying, so the cutlets contain wheat by definition. Croquettes and minced-meat cutlets on the menu are breaded the same way.

As a frying-focused shop with multiple breaded items (loin cutlet, filet cutlet, minced cutlet, croquette) sharing the same oil, cross-contamination with wheat is expected. There is no indication of a dedicated gluten-free fryer.

The meals come with miso soup, pickles, and a house tonkatsu sauce, which typically rely on soy sauce, dashi, and other wheat- and soy-containing seasonings. Most Japanese soy sauce contains wheat, so the sauce and soup should be treated as not gluten-free.
Not vegan-friendly. This is a pork-cutlet shop where the menu is built around fried pork; sides such as miso soup commonly use fish-based dashi and there are no documented plant-based mains.

This is not a celiac-safe kitchen. The menu is built on wheat: bread for the egg and ham-egg sandwiches, spaghetti (Italian and curry spaghetti), and curry rice whose roux is typically flour-based. In a small kissaten kitchen, assume shared surfaces and cross-contact throughout.
Fried items such as katsu curry and croquette curry mean breaded, wheat-coated foods are fried here; no dedicated gluten-free fryer or prep is indicated.

Japanese-style dishes here (e.g., teriyaki pork rice bowl, fried rice, hayashi rice) rely on standard seasonings; most Japanese soy sauce and Worcestershire-style sauces contain wheat, so these should be considered to contain gluten unless the shop confirms otherwise.

No vegan or vegetarian options are indicated. Signature items center on egg (egg sandwich, dry curry with egg), dairy (cream soda, milk in coffee drinks), and meat (beef hayashi rice, pork, cutlets). The curry and hayashi rice are made with beef, and shared cookware makes vegan cross-contact likely.
